article.title: Finding and Dealing with Undirected Systemic Evil

abstract.para: Sometimes systemic evil comes about by accident through well-intentioned individuals. Here's how it happens and what you can do about it.

sect1.title: Introduction to Undirected Systemic Evil
sect1.para: Systemic evil is evil that exists within an organization, or system. There are many obvious instances of systemic evil - Naziism, segregation, etc. These are all easy targets to attack and criticize. However, there is another kind of systemic evil that is more pervasive and harder to control. This kind of systemic evil occurs when good people do good things with good intentions, but the long-term results end up being harmful. Also, it occurs when people aren't doing anything wrong, but neither are they doing anything right. Systemic evil is often the cause when someone has been wronged, but there is noone who is responsible. The book The Grapes of Wrath paints a perfect picture of systemic evil in action in its description of the trials of midwestern farmers in the great depression. The bankers and other people who actually owned the land would send a spokesperson to the land tenants. The spokesperson would tell the tenants to leave the land, because they were late on their payments, or the land was being sold. The tenants were being wronged, but it wasn't by anybody. The spokesperson was only the messenger. The men who ran the bank didn't like the situation, either. They just have a job, and this is what their job told them to do. The people who bought the land from the bank weren't at fault either because they weren't the ones who evicted the original tenet. Although the tenets were being wronged, it is unclear who was acting inappropriately. It appears the system was making evil from the actions of well-intentioned people. I will call it undirected systemic evil, because it does not have an evil source directing the wrongs.

Undirected systemic evil comes from rules that make it impossible to do right. For example, stiff rules by insurance companies on what drugs they allow can often prevent people from getting medication they need. The people who make the rules are probably doing their best to include necessary medication. The people implementing the rules are trying to do their best to keep the business running. However, that can leave people without proper medication. The rules are creating an environment that prevents people from doing the right thing. The goal of this paper is to identify what kinds of rules lead to undirected systemic evil, and how rules can be created which do not have such results.

sect2.title: Situations Changing while Rules Remain Constant
sect2.para: Situations change. What was true yesterday may be different today, and what was considered an unchangeable law of nature in the past may be a joke to future generations. Rules that at one time were beneficial often become burdensome. If affirmative action remains in place after racial discrimination has been purged from society, then it will become a rule that creates boundaries between people rather than heals them. Many of the laws enacted during the depression, although they may have been helpful at the time, stayed around for far too long and dragged the economy behind and consumed taxpayer money, rather than help the economy. This is because they had outlived their usefulness. The situation changed, but the rule remained in place.

sect2.title: Rules Having Unforseen Consequences
sect2.para: Life is complex. It is impossible to know the total effects of any rule or action. Rules can have consequences that noone could have guessed.

sect2.title: Rules Created Too High Up
sect2.para: Many people mistakenly believe that rules can be made which apply everywhere. God may be able to make such rules, but humans cannot. For example, noone should ever make nationwide rules that affect how schools are run day-to-day. The diverse needs of communities and students prevent any set of rules that could be applicable across them all. Attempting to do so only creates problems for local schools. Some schools might benefit, but it might prevent other schools from working which were fine beforehand. In law, some rules are appropriate at the national level, but most are only beneficial when applied on a state or local level, or even left to the choice of individuals. In business rules are made at many levels as well. Some are company-wide, others are by department. Making a decision at the wrong level will always lead to some form of systemic evil.

sect2.title: Not giving people in the field the authority to do what is right
sect2.para: The people who use rules on a daily basis have the most information with which to make decisions. They are the ones who know for sure whether or not a given rule or decision will adversely affect others. Loan officers know best when a bank policy hurts families. Social workers are best able to see where laws and rules break down. Teachers can see where school policy is misinformed. The problem is that frequently these people have no way to make exceptions in order to do the right thing. A teacher might know what's right for his student. However, if that breaks school policy, what does he do? Is he allowed to make an exception? If not, does he have access to someone who can? If the answer to both of these are no, then it is a no-win situation.

sect1.title: Defeating Undirected Systemic Evil from the Source
sect1.para:
Undirected systemic evil comes from the rules and laws we make in good faith. The best way of overcoming this is to be careful when making rules that they don't lend themselves to becoming burdensome on others. In looking at the causes of undirected systemic evil, I've come up with the following guidelines for rule-making to prevent many cases.
For every rule or law made, give a date in which it must be re-evaluated. Make it part of the rule. Noone is perfect and situations change. This makes sure that laws always remain current and useful. You might also include with the rule the reason for the rule and any conditions which would make it not useful.
When creating rules, always make sure that there is some way for an exception to be made, preferably by an individual. Make sure that this person is accessible by those who need him. This way, if exceptions are being made in an obviously poor fashion, then it is obvious who the problem is. Commitees generally make good rules and bad exceptions. Also, be sure that whoever is able to make exceptions is evaluated on a regular basis.
Push the authority for a law as low as possible. As mentioned previously, rules about day-to-day operations of a school should not even be discussed on a national level. If changes need to be made, they should be made on a locality-by-locality basis, even if every school needs changing. This way, each rule or law can follow local community conventions, rather than having inadequate rules made too high up.
Remember that each person has different needs, and needs to be treated differently. Many people think that everyone needs to be treated the same. This actually gives more bias than treating people different. When you treat people the same you ignore their differences, and so the way you treat them will benefit some and harm others. Obviously turning everything into a special case has disadvantages. Pretending everyone has the same needs can be harmful as well. Striking the balance between these two is a difficult challenge.

sect1.title: Battling Systemic Evil from the Outside
sect1.para:
It is more difficult to fight systemic evil without being a policy maker. These are the steps to use for detecting and removing it.
Identify the situation that needs fixing. Think about both how it is currently turning out, and how it should turn out.
Identify which set of rules are causing the situation.
Find out the reason for that set of rules. Usually there is a good motive behind them, or at least one that seemed reasonable at the time. Determine if the motivation is no longer relevant or if a special exception is needed.
Find out who is responsible for the rule - both who created it and who has the power to change it.
Find both parties and alert them to the situation. Don't call the rules "evil" as that probably will give the wrong impression. Just show what purpose the rules were originally for and how they are affecting the particular cases you have in mind. You may make suggestions from the previous list on how to avoid such circumstances in the future.
The rest is up to you and your conscience!
Remember that not every bad situation is the result of systemic evil. Sometimes bad things just happen. However, by paying closer attention to what rules we have and what rules we make we can prevent ourselves from accidentally causing evil in the lives of others.
